item.title: A Few Versions of Myself Later
item.description: This would be a long read; please bear with me.
item.content:encoded:
This would be a long read; please bear with me.

Over the years, I have seen different variations of this quote: “You aren't lost; you're just in an uncomfortable stage of your life where your old self is gone, but your new self isn't fully born yet. You're in the midst of transformation.” At some point, I may have even posted it on my WhatsApp status. I always thought I understood its meaning until I lived and experienced it.

And perhaps, it taught me my biggest lessons this year.

I finished my university education in December 2022. While waiting for my clearance, I worked at my sister’s boutique. I was earning money, but I was anxious about my future. I did not know what to do with my life or how to turn the big dreams I had “dreamt up” in school into reality. It did not help that I studied a course that could not translate into a job or anything with any semblance of one. It’s one of those courses where you only realise you made a huge mistake studying it during your matriculation.

By 2023, it was clear I had a very real problem. I had finished clearance and still didn’t know what to do with my life. I had started applying for entry-level corporate positions, but never heard back from any of them. This was with my then caricature of a CV. I was under a lot of pressure. It felt like time for me to be somebody was quickly running out, and I was playing catch-up. That was until I saw PiggyVest’s opening for a People Operations Associate. I knew I could not apply; I did not have the requisite experience. But for the first time, I was intrigued by a career path.

I read through the job ad thoroughly and went further to read about HR in general, how to get into the field, where to take courses, and what books to read. Before I knew it, I had completed three courses, volunteered for some organisations, and was looking for my first opportunity. I had also used some LinkedIn profiles to map out what my career could look like if I stayed the course. The skills I needed to have a grasp of. The proper certifications to take. You know, the whole nine yards.

The point is, I was so sure that HR was my life’s mission, my life’s work.

By the end of 2023, I got my first HR opportunity as an HR assistant. Oh, I gave it my all and then some. After all, my life’s work deserved nothing short of the best. It got to a point where my manager, the head of HR, who was going on maternity leave, decided not to hire an experienced interim as planned because she was convinced I could handle it.

And so, for the next three months, I was the interim HR manager of an organisation with a workforce of over 400. By the end of that period, I was promoted to an HR Generalist, with rumours of a possible talent manager promotion. This was all within two years.

Life should be good, right? It was not.

Beneath all that work, I would occasionally catch myself feeling dissatisfied and asking if that was it. But I was always either too busy or too tired to give it proper thought.

By June 2025, I resigned from the job. I was thoroughly burned out. My capacity to perform struggled to keep up with the growth I was experiencing. More importantly, life had become so busy that I no longer had time for the things that brought me joy. The very things that allowed me to show up at work the way I did.

So I left, deciding to rest properly before re-entering the job market. During that quiet, dissatisfaction crept up again. Surely, what I had experienced at my last job could not be it. Shortly after, I started job hunting.

By the start of this year (2026), I had gotten a senior People Operations role that 2023 me would have been over the moon for. A good salary, real exposure to leadership, an opportunity to learn stakeholder management and work in a tech environment that offered real exposure to AI. Yet, I wasn’t excited, and I could not pinpoint why.

Anyways, I took the job. A girl has got to eat, you know. But as soon as I began, I knew I had made a terrible mistake. I was miserable. Something was off, but what exactly? I had no idea.

I found myself calling my senior colleagues to ask them what was next. Was that it? They all gave variations of plans for climbing the HR career ladder. But I think what I really wanted was permission to leave that seemingly perfect job and to understand my sudden lack of interest in HR, which was fast becoming a lack of interest in everything too.

I eventually left because I felt I was not giving my best. And I wasn’t, and still am not, the girl who doesn’t give her best. That has never been me. I still thank God for the privilege of having been able to leave.

Retrospectively, I think that was the point I let go of that version of myself and her dreams.

Then came the real anxiety. I had perpetual low energy; nothing brought me joy, and all I wanted to do was sleep. I kept reaching for anything and anyone that would make sense. The recurring question became: why was this happening to me?

I was in that state of mind for a major part of this year. I was also chronically online, watching what felt like thousands of videos on what to do when you don’t know what to do with your life. It felt like 2023 all over again. Only this time, it felt worse because I actually had an amazing job and had just let it go.

Anyways, watching those videos left me more confused than I already was. I desperately needed to hear my own thoughts. So, as my last act of hope, I left all social media platforms. LinkedIn included. I downloaded Substack, just to read and write. Those were the only things that made sense.

After some time, I realised that even though I may not have known exactly what I wanted to do, I knew it had to do with writing. It was the one constant in my life, from keeping journals in secondary school and through university to growing my LinkedIn account to over 13,000 followers, just by writing about my experiences as I learnt HR.

I tried ghostwriting, built a portfolio and set up a whole system, but it never went beyond that. Then I tried proposal and grant writing. It also did not go anywhere, due to my lack of interest, I presume.

You must know that all my life, my effort has always been in the direction of my interest. Always. It was and still is my litmus test for the things I want out of life.

Well, I soldiered on until the day I had a conversation with ChatGPT about technical writing. I can't remember where I heard about it first, but I remember having an insatiable appetite for reading anything and everything related to the field.

Before I knew it, I was done with The Insider’s Guide to Technical Writing by Krista Van Laan. An incredible book, as an aside. It led me to join the Write the Docs Slack community for tech writers. Soon, I had completed a three-course specialisation on Coursera.

I had also written a four-part user guide on getting started on a stock trading app called Meritrade, including FAQs and a style guide, as my unofficial portfolio samples. All written with Markdown in VS Code.

What's funny is that I can’t remember the exact day or time when my world started to feel right again. When I started feeling like me. When everything seemed to be in its place and I stopped feeling confused about life. I genuinely cannot remember.

It's almost like I woke up one day and found all this evidence of what I had been pouring my energy into for the past couple of months.

Clearly, I am not the same girl from January. That girl is long gone, and that's fine because I really like her replacement. Not just because she swapped dreams, but because of the changes she has made in other aspects of her life too.

So, my takeaways?

Firstly, I now know enough to understand that just because someone explains their experience to me in a language we both speak and understand, whether verbally or in a written format like a quote, does not mean I truly understand it. There is a certain level of empathy or perspective I can never have until the experience is a shared one.

Secondly, there was no way I could have known that I was between versions of myself. We only recognise it retrospectively, after we have settled into a new version of ourselves. It's beyond our control. I suspect I have a few more versions of myself to get through. So, in the future, I will pay attention, allow myself to go through it, feel my feelings like my friend would always advise, and not always try to make sense of things.

Also, while writing that last sentence, I realised I had experienced this earlier in life, when my first relationship ended, along with everything I thought I wanted from one.

I think the lesson life has been desperately trying to teach me is that I am allowed to change my mind. About people, beliefs, ideas and things. I am allowed to outgrow relationships, convictions, ambitions and even things I once worked incredibly hard to become. Changing my mind does not mean I was wrong to have wanted those things in the first place. And it certainly isn't evidence that something is wrong with me.

I think I've finally accepted that.

And I think you should too.

item.title: Where Will Tomorrow’s Experienced Professionals Come From?
item.description: For decades, organizations in different sectors have carefully set up systems that cover the supply, training, and eventual retention of entry-level employees. In some sectors, this system is formal and highly standardized, like graduate trainee programmes, which involve job rotations, mentorship, simulations and defined learning pathways. This is particularly popular in the banking sector. In other sectors, the system is less formal. In some cases, the mandatory one-year NYSC supplies entry-level workers, while training happens informally through intentional mentorship and training provided by assigned managers.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, organizations in different sectors have carefully set up systems that cover the supply, training, and eventual retention of entry-level employees. In some sectors, this system is formal and highly standardized, like graduate trainee programmes, which involve job rotations, mentorship, simulations and defined learning pathways. This is particularly popular in the banking sector. In other sectors, the system is less formal. In some cases, the mandatory one-year NYSC supplies entry-level workers, while training happens informally through intentional mentorship and training provided by assigned managers.

These systems, whether formal or less formal, when done right, have been successful in producing solid entry-level employees who go on to become the experienced professionals needed to replace mid-level workers as they move up the career ladder or move on to other things. This is how organizations have ensured a cycle of continuity in the workforce.

For example, my first professional job after school was in a multinational with over 400 employees. I worked as an HR intern in the Human Resources department. It turned out that a lot of the work I had to do involved using spreadsheets (Microsoft Excel), and I had no prior experience with the software. I had to learn. My manager recommended online resources, and with the help of the company’s Data Analyst, I was able to get up to speed.

I also remember being assigned work that involved a lot of research. I would spend hours moving from one website to another, looking for articles relevant to my research. I remember being advised to maintain an empty Word document where I could save relevant links and also use it for brainstorming. Sometimes, the work required me to compare employee benefits and prepare detailed reports for management. My drafts would usually go through several rounds of review before the final document was approved for presentation.

On some days, I would spend all night preparing PowerPoint slides, designing graphics to celebrate employee milestones, or editing videos after a team bonding activity. All of these were in addition to the responsibilities in my actual job description.

I will be honest: I hated the entry-level phase of my career. I hated the grunt work that came with it. It was not glamorous, but it taught me how to work. It taught me to use tools I was not familiar with before and to sit with the discomfort of not getting something right the first time until I did. It taught me how to synthesize information, think critically, and exercise good judgment. It taught me many of the things that make me a good mid-level professional today.

This is the ROI organizations get for investing in entry-level workers: a continuous supply of experienced professionals to fill gaps as mid-level workers move up and senior professionals retire.

Well, fast forward to today. AI has entered the conversation, with the capacity to give us far more for less in minutes. With the right prompts, research, PowerPoint slides, video editing, automation of repetitive tasks, data analysis, writing, document editing, graphic design, and much more can now be done in minutes.

And organizations, in a bid to optimize for efficiency and minimize costs, introduced AI into the very system they created to ensure they always have capable talent.

General tasks that were once associated with entry-level roles are now being handled by AI. In specific fields, AI has also changed the way work is done. For example, AI has been introduced into various aspects of recruitment and software development, where it has given rise to what is commonly called vibe coding. Today, AI can even join a meeting as a participant, give updates, receive feedback, and use that feedback to iterate on assigned work, much like an actual employee.

The result is that, in some fields and organizations, AI is reducing the need for certain junior roles or the number of people required to perform tasks previously assigned to them. And where entry-level positions still exist, the nature of the work has changed.

There is already some research pointing to this shift. A working paper by researchers at Stanford University's Digital Economy Lab, using payroll data covering millions of US workers, found that employment among young workers aged 22 to 25 in occupations highly exposed to AI was 19% below the level it would have reached if it had grown at the same rate as employment in less AI-exposed occupations. Interestingly, the researchers attributed much of this difference to reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased layoffs.

A separate analysis by the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas, using US Census Bureau data, found a similar pattern: employment among younger workers in highly AI-exposed occupations had declined, with fewer young people moving into these jobs.

While these findings do not establish that AI is solely responsible for the decline, they point to a growing concern: the impact of AI may be felt not only through the jobs it replaces, but also through the entry-level opportunities organizations no longer create.

So the question is, in light of the not-so-recent changes brought about by AI, how do we ensure continuity in the workforce when the system previously designed to train entry-level employees and develop solid professionals has been changed unintentionally?

In my opinion, I do not think the introduction of AI is the problem. The issue is that organizations have failed to go back to the drawing board to redesign the systems used to train entry-level employees and rethink how work is structured in light of AI usage. We need to find a way to ensure the coexistence of innovations such as AI and entry-level roles. It should never be one or the other, as is happening today.

Also, the onus is not just on organizations. This responsibility extends to schools as well.

The making of a solid professional does not start with or depend solely on the training provided to entry-level employees by organizations. It starts way before that, in school. Students who will be expected to use AI at work in the future should be encouraged to start using it in school. This preparation should begin long before they become entry-level employees. Yes, I know this is not straightforward. There are risks to consider, and that is a whole different conversation. The point is that school curricula should change as frequently as needed to accommodate the realities of the job market.

I have also found that curriculum review practices vary across education systems. According to an OECD report, some countries undertake major curriculum reforms as needed, while others follow fixed cycles, commonly between five and ten years. In Nigeria, for instance, the NUC recommends that engineering and technology programmes be reviewed at least once every five years. However, given the pace of technological change and its impact on the job market, I think institutions need to pay closer attention to how frequently their curricula are reviewed, updated, and implemented.

Anyway, all of this is to help us recognize that we all have a collective responsibility. The consequences of continuing on this path could be a future with retired senior professionals, few or no mid-level professionals to replace them, and unemployed entry-level workers.

AI is not the enemy, and frankly, I think it is here to stay. So instead of spending time coming up with think pieces (no offence to those who write them) focused on telling entry-level workers how to adapt to today's market, we should all begin to think about the changes that need to happen at a systemic level to ensure that the workforce remains self-replenishing.

item.title: How Online Payments Work
item.content:encoded:
Introduction​

Nigeria has come a long way with payments. From manual bank payments, where we queued for hours, to early mobile/internet banking, to the rise of online payments that fuelled the explosion of online shopping.

You can buy anything online these days, from foodstuff to gadgets, without leaving your home, yet many people don't know how online payments work and often wonder how they work. Well, you are about to find out.

To fully understand how online payments work, you need to understand payment service providers, payment gateways, and webhooks.

Payment service providers (PSP):​

They are companies that own and provide the technology (payment gateway and payment processor) businesses use to collect payments from customers online. They make it possible for you to shop and pay online.
Some of them include:

  • Paystack,
  • Flutterwave,
  • PayU,
  • Seerbit and others.

Payment Gateway​

A payment gateway is the technology that lets a business accept online payments. It securely collects and encrypts a customer’s payment details at checkout, whether by card, bank transfer, or another method, and passes them to the payment processor, which completes the transaction with the customer’s bank.

The exact steps through which this happens are a bit complicated and different for each online payment option, but let's look at how a card payment works.

Sarah’s clothing vendor is running a website sale. To shop, she opens the website, selects a few items, chooses card payment, enters her card details, and completes the payment.

To walk through the process by which the payment gateway ensures Sarah’s payment gets to her vendor, you need to understand the following:​

  • Encryption: this process secures Sarah’s card details so only the necessary parties can access them.

  • Issuing bank: this is Sarah’s bank; she has an account with them. They issued the debit and credit card whose details she entered during checkout.

  • Payment Processor: the part of the payment service provider that receives encrypted card details from the payment gateway, sends them to the issuing bank for authorization, and returns an approval or decline.

  • Authorization: the process by which Sarah’s bank checks whether she has enough funds in her account for the items she wants to buy and whether her account has any restrictions.

  • Acquiring bank: this is the bank that receives and holds payment made through a debit or credit card on behalf of the payment service provider till they send it to Sarah’s vendor’s account.

  • Settlement: this is when Sarah’s bank moves the required amount from her account to the payment service provider’s bank, called the acquiring bank.

Now that we are familiar with these concepts, let’s walk through the simplified version of how a payment gateway ensures that Sarah’s vendor receives her payment.​

  1. The gateway receives Sarah’s card details and encrypts them.

  2. The gateway sends the encrypted data to the provider’s payment processor.

  3. The payment processor sends an authorization request to the issuing bank (Sarah’s bank).

  4. The issuing bank checks Sarah’s account to see whether it has enough funds to cover the items she wants to buy. It also checks that her account isn't frozen or restricted due to fraud.

  5. The issuing bank approves or declines the payment based on the results of these checks.

  6. The payment processor passes the result back to the gateway, which shows Sarah a message on her screen: “Payment successful” or “Payment failed.”

  7. At the same time, the payment service provider sends a webhook to the vendor’s server, so the vendor knows the payment went through and can process Sarah’s order.

  8. Later, usually within a day or two, the issuing bank (Sarah’s bank) sends the required amount to the payment service provider’s acquiring bank. This transfer is called settlement.

  9. The payment service provider sends the money to Sarah’s vendor’s bank account.

Webhook​

In step 7, we mentioned a webhook. Let’s look at it from the vendor’s perspective. How does Sarah’s vendor find out that her payment was successful? That’s where a webhook comes in. A webhook is an automated message from a payment service provider to the vendor’s server.

It is sent when something happens on the provider’s platform that affects the vendor, such as a payment succeeding or failing, a settlement being made, or a refund being issued, among others.

Conclusion​

Now you understand the basics of how online payments work, from the role of payment service providers and payment gateways to how webhooks keep businesses informed about transactions.
